entries.zh: 夫乾坤定位，男女流形，伉儷之義同歸，貴賤之名異等。
entries.en: Heaven and earth fixed their stations; men and women took their bodily shapes. Husband and wife share one moral purpose, even though rank divides high from low.
entries.literal: As for Qian and Kun taking their positions, male and female receive their forms; the principle of husband and wife aims at the same end, yet the names of noble and base stand in different ranks.

entries.zh: 若乃作配皇極，齊體紫宸，象玉床之連後星，喻金波之合羲璧。
entries.en: Those who match the sovereign on high and share the body politic of the inner palace are figured as the jade couch tied to the queen’s asterism, as moonlight married to the solar disk.
entries.literal: When one is paired with the supreme apex and shares the substance of the Purple Palace, it is likened to the jade couch linking to the rear stars, and compared to golden waves joining the Xi disk.

entries.zh: 爰自敻古，是謂元妃；
entries.en: In deepest antiquity she was known as the principal wife;
entries.literal: From remote antiquity onward, she was called the chief consort;

entries.zh: 降及中年，乃稱王后。
entries.en: Later ages styled her queen.
entries.literal: Descending to middle antiquity, she was then titled queen.

entries.zh: 四人並列，光于帝嚳之宮；
entries.en: Four consorts stood side by side and brought glory to Emperor Ku’s inner court;
entries.literal: Four women stood ranked together, shining in the palace of Emperor Ku;

entries.zh: 二妃同降，著彼有虞之典。
entries.en: Two royal brides arrived together and entered the canonical record of Shun’s reign.
entries.literal: Two consorts descended together, written into the canons of Yu’s age.

entries.zh: 夏商以上，六宮之制，其詳靡得而聞焉。
entries.en: For ages before Xia and Shang, no reliable detail survives about how the six wings of the harem were ordered.
entries.literal: Above Xia and Shang, the regulations of the Six Palaces cannot be heard of in detail.

entries.zh: 姬劉以降，五翟之規，其事可略而言矣。
entries.en: From the Zhou and Han dynasties on, the graded “five pheasant” ritual for consorts can at least be sketched.
entries.literal: From Ji and Liu onward, the rules of the five pheasant insignia may be spoken of in outline.

entries.zh: 周禮，天子立一后、三夫人、九嬪、二十七世婦、八十一御妻，以聽王者內政。
entries.en: The Rites of Zhou prescribe one empress, three chief consorts, nine ranked ladies, twenty-seven secondary wives, and eighty-one attendants to manage the sovereign’s domestic government.
entries.literal: In the Rites of Zhou, the Son of Heaven establishes one queen, three ladies, nine bin, twenty-seven wives of rank, and eighty-one minor wives, to administer the king’s inner administration.

entries.zh: 故婚義曰：「天子之與后，如日之與月，陰之與陽。」
entries.en: The Meaning of Marriage therefore declares: “The emperor and his empress mirror sun and moon, yin and yang.”
entries.literal: Therefore the Meaning of Marriage says: “The Son of Heaven and the queen are like sun and moon, yin and yang.”

entries.zh: 由斯而談，其所從來遠矣。
entries.en: Judged by such language, their institution reaches far back into antiquity.
entries.literal: From this perspective, what they derive from is distant indeed.

entries.zh: 故能母儀天宇，助宣王化，德均載物，比大坤維，宗廟歆其薦羞，穹壤俟其交泰。
entries.en: Hence she sets the maternal standard for the realm, advances the king’s civilizing work, and bears creation as steadfastly as earth itself; the temple accepts her sacrifices gladly, and heaven and earth look to her union with the throne for peace.
entries.literal: Thus she can be the motherly model for all under heaven, aid in spreading royal transformation, her virtue evenly bearing all things, comparable to the great sustaining power of Kun; the ancestral temple delights in her offerings, heaven and earth await her harmonizing union.

entries.zh: 是以哲王垂憲，尤重造舟之禮；
entries.en: That is why enlightened monarchs codify law and prize above all the royal wedding rite of “meeting across the boat.”
entries.literal: Therefore wise kings hang forth statutes and especially esteem the rite of the built bridge;

entries.zh: 詩人立言，先獎葛覃之訓。
entries.en: The Classic of Poetry opens by honoring the lessons of “Ge Tan,” the ode on diligent royal ladies.
entries.literal: The poets set forth words and first praise the instruction of “Ge Tan.”

entries.zh: 後燭流景，所以裁其宴私；
entries.en: Dimming the late-night lamp curbs excess in the privy chamber;
entries.literal: The rear candle’s flowing light is the means to regulate their private banquets;

entries.zh: 房樂希聲，是用節其容止。
entries.en: Sparse music in the inner rooms reins in conduct at court and couch alike.
entries.literal: Chamber music with sparse sound is the means to moderate their bearing.

entries.zh: 履端正本，抑斯之謂歟！
entries.en: Walking straight to set the root right—surely this is what those measures intend!
entries.literal: Walking upright to rectify the root—is this not what is meant!

entries.zh: 若乃娉納有方，防閑有禮，肅尊儀而修四德，體柔範而弘六義，陰教洽于宮闈，淑譽騰於區域。
entries.en: When matches are arranged by rule, propriety fences passion, majesty guards ritual while the four womanly virtues are cultivated, gentle models enlarge the six canonical lessons, inner-chamber teaching fills the harem, and fair fame spreads beyond the capital.
entries.literal: If betrothal and intake have proper method, fences and restraint have ritual, reverently honoring ceremony while cultivating the four virtues, embodying gentle norms while extending the six meanings, then women’s instruction permeates the palace, and good reputation rises through the regions.

entries.zh: 則玄雲入戶，上帝錫母萌之符；
entries.en: Then auspicious clouds cross the threshold and Heaven grants the token of fruitful motherhood;
entries.literal: Then dark clouds enter the door, and the Supreme Lord grants the sign of motherhood’s sprouting;

entries.zh: 黃神降徵，坤靈贊壽丘之道，終能鼎祚惟永，胤嗣克昌。
entries.en: The divine Yellow Emperor sends portents; earth’s spirit blesses the birth-hill of sage-kings; the dynasty’s mandate endures and heirs thrive.
entries.literal: The Yellow Spirit sends down omens; the spirit of Kun assists the way of Shouqiu; ultimately the tripod fortune can be everlasting and heirs flourish.

entries.zh: 至若儷極虧閑，憑天作孽，倒裳衣于衽席，感朓側於弦望。
entries.en: But women who reach the throne yet abandon modesty, who invoke Heaven while plotting harm, who turn proper dress upside down on the bed, and whose passions shift with every phase of the moon—
entries.literal: As for those paired to the apex yet deficient in restraint, who rely on heaven to work calamity, who overturn upper and lower garments upon the mat, and feel lust askew at first quarter and full moon.

entries.zh: 則龍漦結釁，宗周鞠為黍苗；
entries.en: —dragon spit seals a fatal feud, and the Zhou heartland turns to weed-grown ruin;
entries.literal: Then dragon-spittle knots disaster, and royal Zhou becomes nothing but millet shoots;

entries.zh: 燕尾挻災，隆漢墜其枌社矣。
entries.en: swallow-tail charms invite catastrophe, and even mighty Han loses its soil-and-millet shrines.
entries.literal: Swallow tails draw calamity, and flourishing Han drops its mulberry altars.

entries.zh: 自曹劉內主，位以色登，甄衛之家，榮非德舉。
entries.en: Under the Cao and Liu courts, palace ladies rose by looks alone; clans such as the Zhens and Weis won favor without moral merit.
entries.literal: Since the inner mistresses of Cao and Liu, position climbed by beauty; in the households of Zhen and Wei, glory was not raised by virtue.

entries.zh: 淫荒挺性，蔑西郊之禮容；
entries.en: Wanton temperaments mocked the solemn suburban liturgy reserved for the empress;
entries.literal: Dissolute and wasteful by nature, they slighted the ritual bearing of the western suburb;

entries.zh: 婉孌含辭，作南國之奇態。
entries.en: Soft voices and studied phrases invented the freakish grace of southern entertainers.
entries.literal: Soft loveliness holding coy phrases, they fashioned exotic manners of the southern states.

entries.zh: 詖謁由斯外人，穢德於是內宣。
entries.en: Sycophancy leaked beyond the palace gates while depravity was preached inside.
entries.literal: Slanderous flattery thereby passed outward, and foul conduct was proclaimed within.

entries.zh: 椒掖播晨牝之風，蘭殿絕河雎之響。
entries.en: The harem aired the omen of women ruling like crowing hens; orchid halls no longer echoed the chaste songs of “Guan ju.”
entries.literal: The pepper chambers spread the wind of the hen crowing at dawn; the orchid halls cut off the echo of “Guan ju” by the River.

entries.zh: 永言彤史，大練之範逾微；
entries.en: Forever the palace diarists wrote, yet the ideal of homespun austerity faded;
entries.literal: Speaking long of the vermilion scribe, the model of coarse white silk grows ever fainter;

entries.zh: 緬視青蒲，脫珥之猷替矣。
entries.en: Looking back to mat audiences where consorts remonstrated, the counsel of tearing off earrings to warn the throne had vanished.
entries.literal: Gazing afar at the green rushes, the strategy of casting off ear-jewels is replaced.

entries.zh: 晉承其末，與世污隆，宣皇創基，功弘而道屈；
entries.en: The Jin took up this fallen era and rose or fell with the times. Emperor Xuan laid the foundations: his deeds were grand, yet the moral course stayed cramped;
entries.literal: Jin inherited the late age; with the world it sank and rose. Emperor Xuan founded the base—achievement broad yet the Way bent;

entries.zh: 穆后一善，勣侔於十亂。
entries.en: a single virtue in Empress Mu rivaled the merit of the “ten turbulent” worthies who saved a dynasty.
entries.literal: one goodness of Empress Mu—merit equal to the Ten Disorderly Ones.

entries.zh: 洎乎世祖，[1]始親選良家，既而帝掩紈扇，躬行請託。
entries.en: Under Emperor Wu [1] the court at first picked brides from respectable houses; soon the sovereign waved his silk fan in the inner quarters and himself traded favors for appointments.
entries.literal: Down to Shizu [1], he began personally selecting from good families; thereafter the emperor hid behind the silk fan and personally practiced solicitation.

entries.zh: 后採長白，實彰妒忌之情；
entries.en: An empress chosen for graying hair laid bare the spite of jealousy;
entries.literal: The empress chose “long white,” truly displaying jealousy;

entries.zh: 賈納短青，竟踐覆亡之轍。
entries.en: the Jias welcomed a young rival and eventually followed the same rut to ruin.
entries.literal: Jia took in “short green,” and in the end trod the rut of overthrow.

entries.zh: 得失遺跡，煥在綈緗，興滅所由，義同畫一。
entries.en: Success and failure still gleam from the silk-bound histories; the springs of fortune and disaster follow one clear pattern.
entries.literal: Tracks of gain and loss shine forth on silk documents; the causes of rise and ruin share one uniform pattern in meaning.

entries.zh: 故列其本事，以為后妃傳云。
entries.en: I therefore set out the essential facts as this “Treatise on Empresses and Consorts.”
entries.literal: Therefore I array their basic affairs to form this treatise on empresses and consorts.

entries.zh: 宣帝初辭魏武之命，託以風痹，嘗暴書，遇暴雨，不覺自起收之。
entries.en: When Emperor Xuan first refused Cao Cao’s summons, claiming crippling palsy, he once aired books in the sun. A cloudburst came; forgetting his act, he leapt up to rescue them.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuan at first declined Wei Wu’s summons, pleading wind paralysis, he once sunned books; encountering a sudden storm, unthinkingly he rose himself to gather them in.

entries.zh: 家惟有一婢見之，后乃恐事泄致禍，遂手殺之以滅口，而親自執爨。
entries.en: A single bondmaid witnessed it. Fearing exposure would destroy them, the empress killed her with her own hands and herself cooked the family meals to hide the truth.
entries.literal: Only one maid in the house saw it; the empress then feared the affair leaking and bringing disaster, so she personally killed her to silence her, and herself attended the cooking stove.

entries.zh: 帝由是重之。
entries.en: Thereafter her husband valued her all the more.
entries.literal: The emperor from this esteemed her.

entries.zh: 其後柏夫人有寵，后罕得進見。
entries.en: Later Lady Bai won his favor, and the empress was seldom admitted.
entries.literal: Afterward Lady Bai had favor, and the empress rarely obtained audience.

entries.zh: 帝嘗臥疾，后往省病。
entries.en: Once when he lay sick, she came to nurse him.
entries.literal: The emperor once lay ill; the empress went to inquire after his illness.

entries.zh: 帝曰：「老物可憎，何煩出也！」
entries.en: He snapped, “That foul old hag—why drag herself here!”
entries.literal: The emperor said: “That old creature is hateful—why trouble to come out!”

entries.zh: 后慚恚不食，將自殺，諸子亦不食。
entries.en: Shamed and furious, she refused food and meant to take her life; her sons fasted with her.
entries.literal: The empress, ashamed and enraged, did not eat and was about to kill herself; her sons likewise did not eat.

entries.zh: 帝驚而致謝，后乃止。
entries.en: Alarmed, he apologized, and she gave up the attempt.
entries.literal: The emperor was alarmed and apologized; the empress then stopped.

entries.zh: 帝退而謂人曰：「老物不足惜，慮困我好兒耳！」
entries.en: Privately he muttered, “I care nothing for the hag—I fear only harm to my fine sons.”
entries.literal: The emperor withdrew and said to someone: “The old creature is not worth pity—I worry she will distress my good sons!”

entries.zh: 后雅有識度，帝每有所為，必豫籌畫。
entries.en: She was poised and far-sighted; whatever her husband planned, she anticipated and shaped.
entries.literal: The empress elegantly had insight and measure; whenever the emperor had something to do, she always planned ahead.

entries.zh: 魏明帝世，宣帝居上將之重，諸子並有雄才大略。
entries.en: Under Wei Mingdi, Sima Yi commanded the armies while his sons showed ruthless ambition.
entries.literal: In Emperor Ming of Wei’s reign, Emperor Xuan occupied the weight of supreme commander; his sons all had heroic talent and broad strategies.

entries.zh: 后知帝非魏之純臣，而后既魏氏之甥，帝深忌之。
entries.en: She knew Sima Yi was no loyal servant of Wei, yet as a Wei princess by birth she herself drew his deepest suspicion.
entries.literal: The empress knew the emperor was not a pure minister of Wei, yet the empress was moreover a niece of the Wei clan—deeply the emperor suspected her.

entries.zh: 青龍二年，遂以鴆崩，時年二十四，葬峻平陵。
entries.en: In 234 she was poisoned at twenty-four and buried at Junping mausoleum.
entries.literal: In the second Qinglong year she then died by poisoned wine, aged twenty-four, buried at Junping tumulus.

entries.zh: 武帝登阼，初未追崇，弘訓太后每以為言，泰始二年始加號諡。
entries.en: After Emperor Wu took the throne he left her unhonored until Empress Dowager Yang at Hongxun repeatedly pressed the matter; only in 266 did he grant posthumous rank and epithet.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, at first he did not posthumously honor her; Empress Dowager Hongxun often spoke of it; only in the second Taishi year did he begin adding title and posthumous name.

entries.zh: 后無男，生五女。
entries.en: She had no sons but five daughters.
entries.literal: The empress had no sons; she bore five daughters.

entries.zh: 宣穆張皇后諱春華，河內平皋人也。
entries.en: Empress Zhang Xuanmu, personal name Chunhua, came from Pinggao in Henei commandery.
entries.literal: Empress Zhang Xuanmu, taboo name Chunhua, was a native of Pinggao in Henei.

entries.zh: 父汪，魏粟邑令；
entries.en: Her father Wang had served as magistrate of Suiyi under Wei;
entries.literal: Her father Wang was magistrate of Suiyi in Wei;

entries.zh: 母河內山氏，司徒濤之從祖姑也。
entries.en: her mother was a Shan from Henei, first cousin once removed to Grand Tutor Shan Tao.
entries.literal: her mother was a Shan of Henei, a paternal grand-aunt by cousinship of Minister of Education Tao.

entries.zh: 后少有德行，智識過人，生景帝、文帝、平原王幹、南陽公主。
entries.en: She showed virtue and unusual discernment from girlhood. She was mother to Emperors Jing and Wen, to Prince Sima Gan of Pingyuan, and to the Princess of Nanyang.
entries.literal: The empress from youth had virtuous conduct and intelligence surpassing others; she bore Emperor Jing, Emperor Wen, Prince Gan of Pingyuan, and the Princess of Nanyang.

entries.zh: 后少聰慧，善書，姿質美麗，閑於女工。
entries.en: From childhood she was bright and graceful, wrote well, was strikingly beautiful, and excelled at needlework.
entries.literal: The empress was clever from youth, skilled at calligraphy, beautiful in bearing, and adept at women’s crafts.

entries.zh: 有善相者嘗相后，當極貴，文帝聞而為世子聘焉。
entries.en: A physiognomist predicted she would rise to the highest rank, and when Emperor Wen heard this he betrothed her to the crown prince.
entries.literal: A skilled physiognomist once read the empress’s features and said she would reach supreme honor; Emperor Wen heard of it and betrothed her to the heir apparent.

entries.zh: 甚被寵遇，生毗陵悼王軌、惠帝、秦獻王柬，平陽、新豐、陽平公主。
entries.en: Deeply favored, she bore Prince Gui of Biling, Emperor Hui, Prince Jian of Qin, and the princesses of Pingyang, Xinfeng, and Yangping.
entries.literal: She received great favor and bore Prince Gui of Biling, Emperor Hui, Prince Jian of Qin, and the princesses of Pingyang, Xinfeng, and Yangping.

entries.zh: 武帝即位，立為皇后。
entries.en: When Sima Yan became emperor, he made her empress.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu took the throne, he established her as empress.

entries.zh: 有司奏依漢故事，皇后、太子各食湯沐邑四十縣，而帝以非古典，不許。
entries.en: Officials asked that, as under Han custom, empress and heir each receive forty bath-fief commanderies, but the emperor refused as non-canonical.
entries.literal: The offices memorialized that, following Han precedent, the empress and crown prince should each receive forty commanderies as bath-and-maintenance fiefs, but the emperor held this was not ancient practice and did not permit it.

entries.zh: 后追懷舅氏之恩，顯官趙俊，納俊兄虞女粲於後宮為夫人。
entries.en: Remembering her uncle’s kindness, she advanced Zhao Jun and took his brother’s daughter Zhao Can into the palace as Honored Lady.
entries.literal: The empress recalled her debt to her mother’s clan, promoted Zhao Jun to high office, and brought Jun’s elder brother’s daughter Can into the inner palace as Honored Lady.

entries.zh: 帝以皇太子不堪奉大統，密以語后。
entries.en: Believing the crown prince unfit to inherit the realm, he confided as much privately to the empress.
entries.literal: The emperor considered the crown prince unable to uphold the great line and secretly spoke of it to the empress.

entries.zh: 后曰：「立嫡以長不以賢，豈可動乎？」
entries.en: She replied, “The eldest legitimate son succeeds regardless of talent—how can we undo that?”
entries.literal: The empress said: “Establishing the heir depends on seniority among legitimate sons, not on talent—how can that be altered?”

entries.zh: 初，賈充妻郭氏使賂后，求以女為太子妃。
entries.en: Earlier Jia Chong’s wife Lady Guo had bribed her to secure her daughter as crown princess.
entries.literal: At first Jia Chong’s wife Lady Guo sent bribes to the empress, seeking to make her daughter crown princess.

entries.zh: 及議太子婚，帝欲娶衛瓘女。
entries.en: When the heir’s marriage came under debate, the emperor favored Wei Guan’s daughter.
entries.literal: When discussing the crown prince’s marriage, the emperor wished to take Wei Guan’s daughter.

entries.zh: 然后盛稱賈后有淑德，又密使太子太傅荀顗進言，上乃聽之。
entries.en: The empress loudly praised Lady Jia’s virtue and secretly had Grand Tutor Xun Yi speak for her, so the emperor yielded.
entries.literal: But the empress greatly praised Consort Jia’s virtuous conduct, and also secretly had Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince Xun Yi speak; the sovereign then consented.

entries.zh: 泰始中，帝博選良家以充後宮，先下書禁天下嫁娶，使宦者乘使車，給騶騎，馳傳州郡，召充選者使后揀擇。
entries.en: Midway through Taishi he cast a wide net for palace women, banned commoners from marrying, sent eunuchs in official carriages with escorts racing along post roads to every commandery, and had the candidates presented to the empress for her verdict.
entries.literal: In the Taishi era the emperor broadly selected good families to fill the rear palace; first he issued a document forbidding marriage in the realm, had eunuchs ride dispatch coaches provided with outriders, gallop relay orders to provinces and commanderies, summon those filling selection and had the empress pick and choose.

entries.zh: 后性妒，惟取潔白長大，其端正美麗者並不見留。
entries.en: Jealous by nature, she kept only plain, towering girls and rejected every truly lovely face.
entries.literal: The empress was by nature jealous; she only took those fair and tall; those properly beautiful were none of them retained.

entries.zh: 時卞藩女有美色，帝掩扇謂后曰：「卞氏女佳。」
entries.en: When Bian Fan’s daughter proved breathtaking, the emperor hid behind his fan and said, “The Bian girl is a jewel.”
entries.literal: At the time Bian Fan’s daughter had beautiful looks; the emperor hid behind a fan and said to the empress: “Bian’s daughter is excellent.”

entries.zh: 后曰：「藩三世后族，其女不可枉以卑位。」
entries.en: The empress answered, “Three generations of Bians have supplied empresses—such a bride cannot be parked in a petty title.”
entries.literal: The empress said: “The Bian clan for three generations has been empress kin—their daughter cannot be slighted with low rank.”

entries.zh: 帝乃止。
entries.en: He dropped the matter.
entries.literal: The emperor then stopped.

entries.zh: 司徒李胤、鎮軍大將軍胡奮、廷尉諸葛沖、太僕臧權、侍中馮蓀、秘書郎左思及世族子女並充三夫人九嬪之列。
entries.en: The daughters of Li Yin, Hu Fen, Zhuge Chong, Zang Quan, Feng Sun, Zuo Si, and other great houses were placed among the Three Ladies and the Nine Concubines.
entries.literal: Minister of Education Li Yin, General Who Guards the Army Hu Fen, Commandant of Justice Zhuge Chong, Grand Coachman Zang Quan, Palace Attendant Feng Sun, Secretary Court Gentleman Zuo Si, and daughters of eminent clans together filled the ranks of three ladies and nine bin.

entries.zh: 司、冀、兗、豫四州二千石將吏家，補良人以下。
entries.en: From Si, Ji, Yan, and Yu the daughters of prefects and local officers filled the ranks below Good Woman.
entries.literal: Families of two-thousand-shi commandery officials in Si, Ji, Yan, and Yu four prefectures supplied ranks below liangren.

entries.zh: 名家盛族子女，多敗衣瘁貌以避之。
entries.en: Great families dressed their girls in rags and smeared their faces to dodge the draft.
entries.literal: Sons and daughters of famous houses and great clans mostly wore tattered clothes and haggard looks to avoid it.

entries.zh: 永嘉元年，追復尊號，別立廟，神主不配武帝。
entries.en: In 307 her title was restored, a separate shrine was built, and her tablet was not enshrined with Emperor Wu.
entries.literal: In the first year of Yongjia her honored title was restored, a separate temple was established, and her spirit tablet was not paired with Emperor Wu.

entries.zh: 至成帝咸康七年，下詔使內外詳議。
entries.en: In 341 Emperor Cheng ordered court and capital officials to deliberate the question fully.
entries.literal: By the seventh year of Xiankang under Emperor Cheng, an edict ordered inner and outer officials to debate the matter in detail.

entries.zh: 衛將軍虞潭議曰：世祖武皇帝光有四海，元皇后應乾作配。
entries.en: Guards General Yu Tan argued: “Emperor Wu illumined the realm; his first empress answered Heaven.”
entries.literal: Guards General Yu Tan argued: “Shizu Emperor Wu glorified the four seas; his primal empress matched Heaven’s pivot.”

entries.zh: 元后既崩，悼后繼作，至楊駿肆逆，禍延天母。
entries.en: After Yang Yan died came Yang Zhi; Yang Jun’s treason dragged down the queen mother.
entries.literal: After the primal empress died, the mourned empress succeeded; when Yang Jun ran riot, calamity reached the Mother of Heaven.

entries.zh: 孝懷皇帝追復號諡，豈不以鯀殛禹興，義在不替者乎！
entries.en: Huai restored her honors—as Gun fell but Yu rose, duty survives.
entries.literal: Emperor Huai restored her title and epithet—is this not because Gun was executed yet Yu rose—the principle of unbroken obligation?

entries.zh: 又太寧二年，臣忝宗正，帝譜泯棄，罔所循按。
entries.en: In Taining 316 I held the clan office; registers were gone.
entries.literal: Moreover in the second Taining year I humbly served as Director of the Imperial Clan; imperial genealogies were lost—nothing to consult.

entries.zh: 時博諮舊齒，以定昭穆，與故驃騎將軍華恒、尚書荀崧、侍中荀邃因舊譜參論撰次，尊號之重，一無改替。
entries.en: With Hua Heng, Xun Song, and Xun Sui we recomposed charts—her rank stood firm.
entries.literal: We broadly queried elders to fix generations and, with former General of Agile Cavalry Hua Heng, Minister Xun Song, Palace Attendant Xun Sui, reviewed old lists to compile order—her lofty title stayed unchanged.

entries.zh: 今聖上孝思，祗肅禋祀，詢及群司，將以恢定大禮。
entries.en: Today’s ruler seeks your counsel to fix court ritual.
entries.literal: Now our sage sovereign’s filial care solemnly tends sacrifice; he asks all bureaus to settle great ritual.

entries.zh: 臣輒思詳，伏見惠皇帝起居注、群臣議奏，列駿作逆謀，危社稷，引魯之文姜，漢之呂后。
entries.en: Hui’s archives cite Wen Jiang and Empress Lü against Yang Jun.
entries.literal: I have reflected carefully: in Emperor Hui’s daily records and ministers’ memorials they listed Jun’s treason, imperiling altars, citing Lu’s Wen Jiang and Han’s Empress Lü.

entries.zh: 臣竊以文姜雖莊公之母，實為父讎；
entries.en: Wen Jiang was Duke Huan’s killer despite bearing Zhuang—
entries.literal: I quietly note that although Wen Jiang was Duke Zhuang’s mother, she was truly her husband’s foe;

entries.zh: 呂后寵樹私戚，幾危劉氏，按此二事異于今日。
entries.en: Empress Lü nearly ruined Han—these differ from Yang Zhi.
entries.literal: Empress Lü favored kin until she nearly ended the Liu house—these two cases differ from today.

entries.zh: 昔漢章帝竇后殺和帝之母，和帝即位盡誅諸竇。
entries.en: Zhangdi’s Dou killed He’s mother; He wiped out the Dous.
entries.literal: Formerly Dou empress of Han Zhangdi killed Emperor He’s mother; when He ascended he slaughtered the Dou clan.

entries.zh: 當時議者欲貶竇后，及后之亡，欲不以禮葬。
entries.en: Critics then sought to shame Dou and withhold burial rites.
entries.literal: Debates then wished to demote Dou empress; when she died some wished denial of ritual burial.

entries.zh: 和帝以奉事十年，義不可違，臣子之道，務從豐厚，仁明之稱，表于往代。
entries.en: He refused cruelty after ten years’ care—his mercy became legend.
entries.literal: He had served her ten years—duty forbade cruelty; ministers pursued lavish burial—his humanity shone for ages.

entries.zh: 又見故尚書僕射裴頠議悼后故事，稱繼母雖出，追服無改。
entries.en: Pei Yi argued Emperor Ai’s mourned empress kept mourning even after divorce.
entries.literal: I also saw former Minister Director Pei Yi’s opinion on Empress Dao’s case—though a stepmother had departed, mourning obligations stayed unchanged.

entries.zh: 是以孝懷皇帝尊崇號諡，還葬峻陵。
entries.en: So Huai restored her posthumous honors at Junling.
entries.literal: Therefore Emperor Huai restored honored title and epithet and reburied her at Jun Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 此則母子道全，而廢事蕩革也。
entries.en: Kin duty survived though politics had fouled them.
entries.literal: Thus mother-son duty stayed whole while violent deeds were swept away.

entries.zh: 于時祭于弘訓之宮，未入太廟。
entries.en: She received offerings only at Hongxun, not the grand temple.
entries.literal: At that time sacrifice occurred at Hongxun Palace—not yet entering the great temple.

entries.zh: 蓋是事之未盡，非義典也。
entries.en: That showed work unfinished, not proper liturgy.
entries.literal: That was because the matter was unfinished—not canonical meaning.

entries.zh: 若以悼后復位為宜，則應配食世祖；
entries.en: If Yang Zhi deserves restoration, she must join Wu’s temple;
entries.literal: If restoring Empress Dao is right, she should share Emperor Wu’s offerings;

entries.zh: 若以復之為非，則譜諡宜闕，未有位號居正，而偏祠別室者也。
entries.en: if not, her titles should lapse—no legitimate rank receives only a side altar.
entries.literal: if restoring her is wrong, then genealogies and epithets should lapse—one cannot hold orthodox rank yet dwell in a side shrine alone.

entries.zh: 若以孝懷皇帝私隆母子之道，特為立廟者，此苟崇私情，有虧國典，則國譜帝諱，皆宜除棄，匪徒不得同祀于世祖之廟也。
entries.en: A private shrine for filial piety alone would break precedent and void every register.
entries.literal: If Emperor Huai privately enlarged mother-son feeling and built a special temple, that would exalt private affection yet wound state canon—then clan registers and temple names should all be discarded, not merely barred from Wu’s temple.

entries.zh: 駿既死，詔使後軍將軍荀悝送后于永寧宮。
entries.en: After Yang Jun fell, Rear-General Xun Kui was ordered to move her to Yongning Palace.
entries.literal: After Jun died, an edict ordered Rear-General Xun Kui to escort the empress to Yongning Palace.

entries.zh: 特全后母高都君龐氏之命，聽就后居止。
entries.en: Her mother Lady Pang was spared and permitted to live with her.
entries.literal: Her mother Lady Pang of Gaodu Commandery was specially spared and allowed to stay with the dowager.

entries.zh: 賈后諷群公有司奏曰：「皇太后陰漸姦謀，圖危社稷，飛箭繫書，要募將士，同惡相濟，自絕于天。
entries.en: Jia’s faction petitioned: “The dowager schemed treason, imperiled the state, shot letters beyond the walls, and recruited troops—criminals helped her and Heaven abandoned her.
entries.literal: Empress Jia prompted assembled dukes and offices to memorialize: “The empress dowager secretly carried treason, plotted against the altars, flew arrows with letters tied, summoned soldiers—wicked men aided her and she cut herself off from Heaven.

entries.zh: 魯侯絕文姜，春秋所許，蓋以奉順祖宗，任至公於天下。
entries.en: Lu cut ties with Wen Jiang, which the Annals condone, to serve ancestors and justice.
entries.literal: Duke Lu cut off Wen Jiang—the Spring and Autumn approves—because one must honor ancestors and hold utmost fairness toward the realm.

entries.zh: 陛下雖懷無已之情，臣下不敢奉詔。
entries.en: We know your grief, sire, yet we cannot sanction mercy.
entries.literal: Although Your Majesty harbors endless feeling, your servants dare not obey the edict.

entries.zh: 可宣敕王公于朝堂會議。」
entries.en: Summon princes and ministers to the outer court for debate.”
entries.literal: Let an order proclaim that kings and dukes convene in the court hall to deliberate.”

entries.zh: 詔曰：「此大事，更詳之。」
entries.en: The throne replied, “Weighty—deliberate further.”
entries.literal: An edict said: “This is a great matter—consider it again.”

entries.zh: 有司又奏：「駿藉外戚之資，居冢宰之任，陛下既居諒闇，委以重權，至乃陰圖凶逆，布樹私黨。
entries.en: They answered: “Yang Jun used kinship to seize power; while you mourned he plotted rebellion and packed offices with clients.
entries.literal: The offices again memorialized: “Jun relied on affinal backing and held prime minister’s charge; while Your Majesty mourned in the dark palace he received heavy trust, yet secretly plotted treason and planted private partisans.

entries.zh: 皇太后內為脣齒，協同逆謀，禍釁既彰，背捍詔命，阻兵負眾，血刃宮省，而復流書募眾，以獎凶黨，上背祖宗之靈，下絕億兆之望。
entries.en: The dowager abetted him; when crime surfaced she resisted orders, armed her faction, and stained the palace—yet still shot appeals to arm traitors, dishonoring spirits and people.
entries.literal: The empress dowager was his lip and tooth within; she joined the wicked plot. Once the stench showed, she defied decrees, blocked armies, and bloodied the palace—yet still flew letters to recruit crowds and reward villains, betraying ancestors above and cutting off the myriad hopes below.

entries.zh: 昔文姜與亂，春秋所貶，呂宗叛戾，高后降配，宜廢皇太后為峻陽庶人。」
entries.en: Like Wen Jiang or Empress Lü, she must be struck from dowager rank and made a commoner of Junyang.”
entries.literal: Formerly Wen Jiang joined turmoil—the Spring and Autumn demoted her; the Lü clan rebelled and Empress Gao was lowered in pairing. She should be demoted from empress dowager to commoner of Junyang.”

entries.zh: 中書監張華等以為「太后非得罪于先帝者也，今黨惡所親，[3]為不母于聖世。
entries.en: Zhang Hua argued: “She never wronged Emperor Wu; siding with villains now breaks maternal duty in our era [3].
entries.literal: Palace Supervisor Zhang Hua and others held: “The dowager did not offend the late emperor; now she joins wicked kin—she fails motherhood toward this sage age [3].

entries.zh: 宜依孝成趙皇后故事，曰武帝皇后，處之離宮，以全貴終之恩。」
entries.en: Treat her like Chengdi’s Zhao—call her Emperor Wu’s consort, lodge her apart, yet grant a decent end.”
entries.literal: She should follow Empress Zhao of Emperor Cheng’s precedent—styled Empress of Emperor Wu and housed in a detached palace to preserve honored kindness to the end.”

entries.zh: 尚書令、下邳王晃等議曰：「皇太后與駿潛謀，欲危社稷，不可復奉承宗廟，配合先帝。
entries.en: Wang Huang countered: “She conspired with Yang Jun—she cannot share Wu’s temple.
entries.literal: Minister Director Prince Kang of Xiapi Huan and others debated: “The empress dowager secretly plotted with Jun to overturn the state—she cannot again serve the temple or pair with the late emperor.

entries.zh: 宜貶尊號，廢詣金墉城。」
entries.en: Strip her titles and lock her in Jinyong.”
entries.literal: Her honored title should be stripped and she banished to Metal-Walled Fortress.”

entries.zh: 于是有司奏：「請從晃等議，廢太后為庶人。
entries.en: Officials petitioned: "We ask to adopt Huang's proposal and depose the dowager as a commoner.
entries.literal: Thereupon the offices petitioned: “We ask following Huang’s proposal—depose the dowager as commoner.

entries.zh: 遣使者以太牢告于郊廟，以奉承祖宗之命，稱萬國之望。
entries.en: Announce it with suburban bull sacrifice to ancestors and satisfy the realm.
entries.literal: Dispatch envoys with grand sacrifice to announce at suburban altars and ancestral temple, obeying ancestor spirits and answering myriad lands’ expectation.

entries.zh: 至於諸所供奉，可順聖恩，務從豐厚。」
entries.en: Let her maintenance stay generous per your mercy.”
entries.literal: As for all provisions supplied, follow sagely kindness and strive for abundance.”

entries.zh: 詔不許。
entries.en: The emperor refused.
entries.literal: The edict did not permit.

entries.zh: 有司又固請，乃可之。
entries.en: They insisted again; he yielded.
entries.literal: The offices pressed again; then he consented.

entries.zh: 又奏：「楊駿造亂，家屬應誅，詔原其妻龐命，以慰太后之心。
entries.en: They added: “Yang Jun’s clan should die; you spared Lady Pang to comfort the dowager.
entries.literal: They also memorialized: “Yang Jun raised rebellion—his kin deserve execution; the edict spared his wife Pang to console the dowager.

entries.zh: 今太后廢為庶人，請以龐付廷尉行刑。」
entries.en: Now that she is a commoner, execute Lady Pang.”
entries.literal: Now that the dowager is demoted to commoner, we ask that Pang be handed to the Commandant of Justice for execution.”

entries.zh: 詔曰：「聽龐與庶人相隨。」
entries.en: He ruled: “Let Lady Pang stay with her.”
entries.literal: The edict said: “Let Pang follow the commoner.”

entries.zh: 有司希賈后旨，固請，乃從之。
entries.en: Bowing to Jia’s will they insisted until he agreed.
entries.literal: The offices, courting Empress Jia’s intent, pressed firmly; then he followed.

entries.zh: 龐臨刑，太后抱持號叫，截髮稽顙，上表詣賈后稱妾，請全母命，不見省。
entries.en: At Lady Pang’s execution the dowager clung to her, cut her hair, kowtowed, signed herself Jia’s servant to beg for mercy—Jia ignored her.
entries.literal: When Pang faced execution, the empress dowager clutched her, wailing; she cut her hair and knocked her forehead, submitted a memorial as concubine to Empress Jia begging to save her mother’s life—she was not granted audience.

entries.zh: 初，太后尚有侍御十餘人，賈后奪之，絕膳而崩，時年三十四，在位十五年。
entries.en: Jia stripped her servants; she starved at thirty-four after fifteen years as consort.
entries.literal: At first the dowager still had more than ten attendants; Empress Jia seized them; she starved and died, aged thirty-four, having held rank fifteen years.

entries.zh: 賈后又信妖巫，謂太后必訴冤先帝，乃覆而殯之，施諸厭劾符書藥物。
entries.en: Jia feared her ghost would accuse Emperor Wu, so she buried her prone under talismans.
entries.literal: Empress Jia further trusted witchcraft, fearing the dowager would appeal her grievance to the late emperor; she therefore buried her face-down with curse charms and drugs.

entries.zh: 會稽王昱、中書監庾冰、中書令何充、尚書令諸葛恢、尚書謝廣、光祿勳留擢、丹楊尹殷融、護軍將軍馮懷、散騎常侍鄧逸等咸從潭議，由是太后配食武帝。
entries.en: Yu Yi, Yu Bing, He Chong, Zhuge Hui, Xie Guang, Liu Zhuo, Yin Rong, Feng Huai, and Deng Yi endorsed Tan—Yang Zhi joined Wu’s temple.
entries.literal: Prince Hui of Kuaiji Yu, Palace Supervisor Yu Bing, Palace Director He Chong, Minister Director Zhuge Hui, Minister Xie Guang, Superintendent of the Household Liu Zhuo, Intendant of Danyang Yin Rong, Defender-general Feng Huai, and Palace Rider Deng Yi all followed Tan’s opinion; thereby the dowager shared Emperor Wu’s sacrifices.

entries.zh: 惟泰始十年秋七月丙寅，晉元皇后楊氏崩，嗚呼哀哉！
entries.en: On that summer day in 274 Jin’s Empress Yang Yan passed—alas!
entries.literal: On the bingyin day of autumn in the seventh month of the tenth Taishi year the Jin primal empress Lady Yang died—alas!

entries.zh: 昔有莘適殷，姜姒歸周，宣德中闈，徽音永流。
entries.en: Youxin wed Yin; Jiang water wed Zhou—inner chambers rang with virtue.
entries.literal: Ancient Youxin married Yin; Jiang Si returned to Zhou—virtue spread within the palace, fair fame forever flows.

entries.zh: 樊衛二姬，匡齊翼楚；
entries.en: Fan Ji and Wei Ji uplifted Qi and Chu;
entries.literal: The two Ji ladies of Fan and Wei steadied Qi and aided Chu;

entries.zh: 馬鄧兩妃，亦毗漢主。
entries.en: Ma and Deng consorts beside Han sovereigns did the same.
entries.literal: the two consorts Ma and Deng likewise aided Han sovereigns.

entries.zh: 峨峨元后，光嬪晉宇。
entries.en: Towering primal queen—you lit the Jin harem.
entries.literal: Lofty primal queen—you glorified consorts of Jin.

entries.zh: 伉儷聖皇，比蹤往古。
entries.en: You walked beside the sage throne as queens of old.
entries.literal: You matched the sage emperor—tracks aligned with ancient models.

entries.zh: 遭命不永，背陽即陰。
entries.en: Heaven refused long life—you crossed from light to shade.
entries.literal: Heaven granted no long span—you turned from yang toward shade.

entries.zh: 六宮號咷，四海慟心。
entries.en: Six wings of the harem keened; all beneath Heaven tore their breasts.
entries.literal: Six palaces wailed; four seas shared torn hearts.

entries.zh: 嗟余鄙妾，銜恩特深。
entries.en: Mean concubine though I am—your kindness pierced deepest.
entries.literal: Alas, mean concubine—I bore uniquely deep grace.

entries.zh: 追慕三良，甘心自沈。
entries.en: I envy the three who followed Duke Mu—I would gladly sink with you.
entries.literal: I chase the Three Worthies—gladly I would sink myself.

entries.zh: 何用存思？
entries.en: Why hoard longing?
entries.literal: What use is longing?

entries.zh: 不忘德音。
entries.en: Keep your virtuous words alive.
entries.literal: Never forget virtuous words.

entries.zh: 何用紀述？
entries.en: Why record deeds?
entries.literal: What use is chronicling?

entries.zh: 託辭翰林。
entries.en: Commit them to ink and Hanlin.
entries.literal: Entrust phrases to the brush grove.

entries.zh: 乃作誄曰：
entries.en: Thus runs her lament:
entries.literal: Thus she composed the dirge, saying:

entries.zh: 赫赫元后，出自有楊。
entries.en: Bright primal queen—you rose from the house of Yang.
entries.literal: Radiant primal queen—you sprang from Yang.

entries.zh: 奕世朱輪，燿彼華陽。
entries.en: Generation on generation rode vermillion wheels—Huayang blazed.
entries.literal: For generations vermillion wheels gleamed—Huayang blazed.

entries.zh: 惟嶽降神，顯茲禎祥。
entries.en: Sacred peaks poured forth spirit—showing these blessed omens.
entries.literal: The peak sent down spirits—revealing these auspicious signs.

entries.zh: 篤生英媛，休有烈光。
entries.en: From them sprang a heroine blazing with light.
entries.literal: Earnestly was born a splendid maid—she bore radiant glory.

entries.zh: 含靈握文，異于庶姜。
entries.en: Spirit and letters dwelt in her—not common flesh.
entries.literal: She housed spirit and grasped pattern—unlike common Jiang brides.

entries.zh: 和暢春日，操厲秋霜。
entries.en: Gentle as vernal sun; resolve sharp as autumn frost.
entries.literal: Gentle as spring sun; carriage stern as autumn frost.

entries.zh: 疾彼攸遂，敦此義方。
entries.en: She spurned reckless ease and upheld righteous paths.
entries.literal: She hated those who rushed heedlessly; she cherished righteous rule.

entries.zh: 率由四教，匪怠匪荒。
entries.en: She walked the four teachings—never idle, never wild.
entries.literal: She followed the four teachings—never slack, never waste.

entries.zh: 行周六親，徽音顯揚。
entries.en: Among six degrees of kin her sweet fame rang.
entries.literal: She moved through six kinships—fair fame rose bright.

entries.zh: 顯揚伊何？
entries.en: Where did her praise ring?
entries.literal: Where did that fame shine?

entries.zh: 京室是臧。
entries.en: It rang through the royal house.
entries.literal: The capital chamber held her good.

entries.zh: 乃娉乃納，聿嬪聖皇。
entries.en: Courtship led her to the sage sovereign’s side.
entries.literal: Betrothed and welcomed—she married the sage emperor.

entries.zh: 正位閨閾，惟德是將。
entries.en: She ordered inner gates—virtue guided every step.
entries.literal: She rectified inner thresholds—virtue led her charge.

entries.zh: 鳴珮有節，發言有章。
entries.en: Her pendants chimed in rhythm; every phrase wore pattern.
entries.literal: Jade pendants sounded with measure; speech carried patterned grace.

entries.zh: 仰觀列圖，俯覽篇籍。
entries.en: She studied charts above and rolled texts below.
entries.literal: She looked up to illustrated charts; bent to scan texts.

entries.zh: 顧問女史，咨詢竹帛。
entries.en: She queried palace scholars and silk-bound histories.
entries.literal: She consulted female scribes; asked counsel of bamboo and silk.

entries.zh: 思媚皇姑，虔恭朝夕。
entries.en: She charmed her royal mother-in-law with dawn-and-dusk reverence.
entries.literal: She sought to charm royal mother-in-law—dawn and dusk reverent.

entries.zh: 允釐中饋，執事有恪。
entries.en: She governed inner kitchens—every duty performed with awe.
entries.literal: She truly ordered inner kitchens—each task performed with awe.

entries.zh: 後為貴嬪，姿陋無寵，以才德見禮。
entries.en: Raised to honorable lady despite plain looks, she won respect through wit and character.
entries.literal: Later she became honorable lady—plain in looks without favor, honored for talent and virtue.

entries.zh: 體羸多患，常居薄室，帝每遊華林，輒回輦過之。
entries.en: Frail and sickly, she kept to spare rooms; each imperial outing to Splendid Grove detoured past her lodge.
entries.literal: Her frame frail and often ill, she dwelt in modest chambers; whenever the emperor toured Splendid Grove he turned his carriage to pass her gate.

entries.zh: 言及文義，辭對清華，左右侍聽，莫不稱美。
entries.en: Her answers on texts sparkled; every listener praised her grace.
entries.literal: When discourse touched literary meaning her replies were lucid and splendid; attendants left and right listened—none failed to praise.

entries.zh: 于禮斯勞，于敬斯勤。
entries.en: Ritual bent her back; reverence drove her nights.
entries.literal: In ritual she toiled; in reverence she strove.

entries.zh: 雖曰齊聖，邁德日新。
entries.en: Though hailed unequaled, her virtue renewed each dawn.
entries.literal: Although called peerlessly holy, her virtue renewed daily.

entries.zh: 日新伊何，克廣弘仁。
entries.en: What did renewal bring?
entries.literal: What meant daily renewal?

entries.zh: 終溫且惠，帝妹是親。
entries.en: Ever-kind, ever-gentle—she cherished the emperor’s own sisters.
entries.literal: She widened lavish kindness—she cherished the emperor’s sisters.

entries.zh: 經緯六宮，罔不彌綸。
entries.en: She threaded six wings of the harem—nothing slipped her weave.
entries.literal: She wove order through six palaces—nothing escaped her net.

entries.zh: 群妾惟仰，譬彼北辰。
entries.en: Lesser ladies looked up as to the North Star.
entries.literal: Concubines looked up as to the pole star.

entries.zh: 亦既青陽，鳴鳩告時。
entries.en: Spring greens when turtle-doves call the hour.
entries.literal: Already green spring—the turtle dove announces season.

entries.zh: 躬執桑曲，率導媵姬。
entries.en: She led brides with mulberry hook in hand.
entries.literal: She grasped mulberry hooks herself—leading attendant brides.

entries.zh: 修成蠶蔟，分繭理絲。
entries.en: She tended trays, split cocoons, sorted filament.
entries.literal: She finished silkworm trays—partitioned cocoons, sorted silk.

entries.zh: 女工是察，祭服是治。
entries.en: She inspected needlework and fashioned sacral gowns.
entries.literal: She inspected women’s work—she directed ritual robes.

entries.zh: 祗奉宗廟，永言孝思。
entries.en: She served the temple—always mindful of filial hearts.
entries.literal: She reverently served the ancestral temple—ever speaking filial thought.

entries.zh: 于彼六行，靡不蹈之。
entries.en: She practiced every womanly virtue.
entries.literal: Of those six conducts—she trod every one.

entries.zh: 皇英佐舜，塗山翼禹。
entries.en: Ehuang and Nüying aided Shun; Tushan aided Yu.
entries.literal: Huang and Ying aided Shun; Tushan winged Yu.

entries.zh: 惟衛惟樊，二霸是輔。
entries.en: Wei Ji and Fan Ji steadied two hegemons.
entries.literal: Only Wei, only Fan—two hegemons relied on them.

entries.zh: 明明我后，異世同矩。
entries.en: Bright our queen—another age, same measure.
entries.literal: Bright bright our queen—different age, same square rule.

entries.zh: 亦能有亂，謀及天府。
entries.en: She too could heal unrest ; she schemed with Heaven’s storehouse.
entries.literal: She too could cope with turmoil ; she planned with Heaven’s treasury.

entries.zh: 內敷陰教，外毗陽化。
entries.en: Within she spread yin teaching; without she aided yang rule.
entries.literal: Within she spread women’s teaching; without she aided yang transformation.

entries.zh: 綢繆庶正，密勿夙夜。
entries.en: She knit every minister—tireless day and night.
entries.literal: She bound together myriad officers—diligent night and day.

entries.zh: 恩從風翔，澤隨雨播。
entries.en: Her grace rode wind; her bounty fell like rain.
entries.literal: Grace rode the wind; bounty fell like rain.

entries.zh: 中外禔福，遐邇詠歌。
entries.en: Court and countryside flourished; near and far sang hymns.
entries.literal: Inner and outer gained bliss—near and far sang praise.

entries.zh: 天祚貞吉，克昌克繁。
entries.en: Heaven kept auspicious fate—family branches multiplied.
entries.literal: Heaven’s mandate stayed auspicious—multiplying, branching wide.

entries.zh: 則百斯慶，育聖育賢。
entries.en: Blessings arrived in hundreds—bearing sage sons and worthy princes.
entries.literal: Thus came hundredfold blessing—bearing sages and worthies.

entries.zh: 教踰妊姒，訓邁姜嫄。
entries.en: Her teaching topped Si and Ren; her norms surpassed Jiang Yuan.
entries.literal: Teaching surpassed Ren and Si; instruction overtook Jiang Yuan.

entries.zh: 堂堂太子，惟國之元。
entries.en: Lofty the heir—pillar of the realm.
entries.literal: Grand stands the crown prince—root of the state.

entries.zh: 濟濟南陽，為屏為藩。
entries.en: Splendid Nanyang princes—screens and river guards.
entries.literal: Splendid princes of Nanyang—screens and hedges for the throne.

entries.zh: 本支菴藹，四海蔭焉。
entries.en: Root and branch spread shade—the realm rests cool.
entries.literal: Root and branch shade thick—four seas rest beneath.

entries.zh: 微斯皇妣，孰茲克臻。
entries.en: Without this queen mother—who could climb so high?
entries.literal: Without this royal mother—who could reach such zenith?

entries.zh: 曰乾蓋聰，曰聖允誠。
entries.en: They call Heaven keen; they call sageness true.
entries.literal: They say Qian is keen; they say sage is true.

entries.zh: 積善之堂，五福所并。
entries.en: Goodness piled high—the five blessings gather.
entries.literal: Hall piled with goodness—five blessings assemble.

entries.zh: 宜享高年，匪隕匪傾。
entries.en: She deserved long years—never to fall or fail.
entries.literal: She should enjoy lofty years—not fall, not tilt.

entries.zh: 如彭之齒，如聃之齡。
entries.en: Like Peng Zu’s span; like Laozi’s age.
entries.literal: Like Peng’s tooth-count; like Dan’s lifespan.

entries.zh: 云胡不造，于茲禍殃[5]。
entries.en: Why deny Heaven’s favor—why strike her here [5]?
entries.literal: Why was fortune not granted—here calamity struck [5]?

entries.zh: 寢疾彌留，寤寐不康。
entries.en: She lingered at death’s door—no sleep brought ease.
entries.literal: Illness lingered at death’s gate—sleep brought no peace.

entries.zh: 巫咸騁術，和鵲奏方。
entries.en: Shaman Wu worked spells; healers He and Que brewed drafts.
entries.literal: Wu Xian wielded arts; He and Bian offered prescriptions.

entries.zh: 祈禱無應，嘗藥無良。
entries.en: Prayers failed; every draught proved vain.
entries.literal: Prayers won no answer; tasted drugs brought no cure.

entries.zh: 形神將離，載昏載荒。
entries.en: Body and soul slipped apart—dimming into gloom.
entries.literal: Body and spirit parted—darkening, wasting.

entries.zh: 奄忽崩殂，湮精滅光。
entries.en: Suddenly she fell—light drowned in dark.
entries.literal: Suddenly she collapsed—spirit sank, light died.

entries.zh: 哀哀太子，南陽繁昌。
entries.en: The heir mourns—the flourishing prince of Nanyang.
entries.literal: Mournful crown prince—Nanyang’s flowering prince.

entries.zh: 攀援不寐，擗踊摧傷。
entries.en: He cannot climb from grief—beats his breast till bones break.
entries.literal: He climbs yet cannot sleep—beats breast and breast is torn.

entries.zh: 嗚呼哀哉！
entries.en: Alas for this sorrow!
entries.literal: Alas, oh grief!

entries.zh: 闔宮號咷，宇內震驚。
entries.en: Every hall keened—the realm inside the seas shook.
entries.literal: Whole palace wailed—the realm within seas trembled.

entries.zh: 奔者填衢，赴者塞庭。
entries.en: Runners clogged roads—mourners packed the yard.
entries.literal: Runners choked the avenues—mourners jammed the courtyard.

entries.zh: 哀慟雷駭，流淚雨零。
entries.en: Mourning crashed like thunder; tears fell like showers.
entries.literal: Grief crashed like thunder—tears fell like rain.

entries.zh: 歔欷不已，若喪所生。
entries.en: No sob ends—as if a parent died.
entries.literal: Sobs cease not—as if parents were lost.

entries.zh: 惟帝與后，契闊在昔。
entries.en: Emperor and queen—pledged long ago.
entries.literal: Emperor and consort—long joined in ancient pledge.

entries.zh: 比翼白屋，雙飛紫閣。
entries.en: They nested in humble roofs—then flew paired to purple halls.
entries.literal: Wing to wing from white-thatched halls—paired flight to purple towers.

entries.zh: 悼后傷后，早即窀穸。
entries.en: They mourn their queen—she sank too soon to stone.
entries.literal: Mourning queen, wounded queen—early she entered the vault.

entries.zh: 言斯既及，涕泗隕落。
entries.en: Speech stops here—tears and mucus fall.
entries.literal: Words reach here—tears and mucus fall.

entries.zh: 追惟我后，實聰實哲。
entries.en: Remembering her—truly keen, truly wise.
entries.literal: Tracing my queen—truly keen, truly wise.

entries.zh: 通于性命，達于儉節。
entries.en: She grasped life’s truth—she mastered austerity.
entries.literal: She penetrated nature and fate—she grasped thrift’s rule.

entries.zh: 送終之禮，比素上世。
entries.en: Her burial honored utmost thrift—plain as oldest times.
entries.literal: Funeral rites matched plain antiquity—pared like highest ages.

entries.zh: 襚無珍寶，唅無明月。
entries.en: Her grave clothes bore no gems; no pearl filled her mouth.
entries.literal: Burial garments held no treasure; mouth jewels held no bright moon-pearl.

entries.zh: 潛輝梓宮，永背昭晰。
entries.en: Her gleam sinks in the catalpa bier—gone from daylight forever.
entries.literal: Hidden radiance in the catalpa palace—forever turned from clear light.

entries.zh: 臣妾哀號，同此斷絕。
entries.en: We servants keened—we shared that rupture.
entries.literal: Concubines and maids wail—together cut off.

entries.zh: 庭宇遏密，幽室增陰。
entries.en: Courtyards fell mute; shadow thickened every room.
entries.literal: Courtyard silence grows dense—dark chambers deepen shade.

entries.zh: 空設幃帳，虛置衣衾。
entries.en: Silken curtains hang hollow; quilts lie unused.
entries.literal: Canopies stand empty—robes and quilts vainly spread.

entries.zh: 人亦有言，神道難尋。
entries.en: Men say ghost roads cannot be traced.
entries.literal: Men also say the spirit path cannot be traced.

entries.zh: 悠悠精爽，豈浮豈沈。
entries.en: Her bright soul wanders—does it rise or sink?
entries.literal: Far drifts her shining soul—does it float or sink?

entries.zh: 豐奠日陳，冀魂之臨。
entries.en: Opulent gifts pile daily—we pray her ghost approaches.
entries.literal: Rich offerings daily spread—we hope the soul draws near.

entries.zh: 孰云元后，不聞其音。
entries.en: Who claims our primal queen hears nothing now?
entries.literal: Who says the primal queen—cannot hear her voice?

entries.zh: 翼翼聖皇，叡喆孔純。
entries.en: Solemn sage emperor—pure in deepest wit.
entries.literal: Solemn sage emperor—profound wisdom utterly pure.

entries.zh: 愍茲狂戾，闡惠播仁。
entries.en: He pitied cruel times—spread mercy everywhere.
entries.literal: He pitied cruel turmoil—spread kindness and planted mercy.

entries.zh: 蠲釁滌穢，與時惟新。
entries.en: He washed sin away—made all things new.
entries.literal: He wiped stains and washed filth—renewed with seasons.

entries.zh: 沛然洪赦，恩詔遐震。
entries.en: Grand amnesty rolled—edicts shook frontiers.
entries.literal: Surging great amnesty—edicts shook distant shores.

entries.zh: 后之踐阼，囹圄虛陳。
entries.en: When she rose—jails gaped empty.
entries.literal: When she mounted throne—prisons stood empty.

entries.zh: 萬國齊歡，六合同欣。
entries.en: Ten thousand states danced—six directions sang.
entries.literal: Ten thousand lands rejoiced—six zones shared delight.

entries.zh: 坤神抃舞，天人載悅。
entries.en: Earth spirit dances—Heaven and mortals thrill.
entries.literal: Earth goddess claps—Heaven and man rejoice.

entries.zh: 興瑞降祥，表精日月。
entries.en: Good omens arrive—sun and moon blaze essence.
entries.literal: Omens rise—sun and moon display essence.

entries.zh: 和氣煙熅，三光朗烈。
entries.en: Warm vapors coil—three lights burn bright.
entries.literal: Harmony veils warm mist—three luminaries blaze clear.

entries.zh: 既獲嘉時，尋播甘雪。
entries.en: Blessed hour brings timely snow.
entries.literal: Season blessed—they soon spread sweet snow.

entries.zh: 玄雲晻藹，靈液霏霏。
entries.en: Purple clouds billow—spirit dew drifts.
entries.literal: Dark clouds veil thick—numinous dew drifts fine.

entries.zh: 既儲既積，待陽而晞。
entries.en: Moisture gathers—sun must dry it.
entries.literal: Stored and piled—it waits for sun to dry.

entries.zh: 曣晛沾濡，柔潤中畿。
entries.en: Warm vapor drenches—capital fields soften.
entries.literal: Moisture soaks—soft rains central fields.

entries.zh: 長享豐年，福祿永綏。
entries.en: Enjoy fat harvests—wealth and peace endure.
entries.literal: Long enjoy rich years—blessing and wage forever calm.

entries.zh: 泰始九年，帝多簡良家子女以充內職，自擇其美者以絳紗繫臂。
entries.en: In 273 he drafted palace girls from good families and marked his favorites with crimson silk arm-bands.
entries.literal: In ninth Taishi year the emperor broadly drafted daughters of good houses for inner service and personally tied crimson gauze on those he deemed fairest.

entries.zh: 而芳既入選，下殿號泣。
entries.en: Hu Fang crossed the hall weeping once chosen.
entries.literal: When Fang entered selection she descended the hall weeping and crying.

entries.zh: 左右止之曰：「陛下聞聲。」
entries.en: Attendants hissed, “The emperor will hear.”
entries.literal: Attendants beside her stopped her: “His Majesty will hear your voice.”

entries.zh: 芳曰：「死且不畏，何畏陛下！」
entries.en: She shot back, “I fear death itself—why fear an emperor?”
entries.literal: Fang said: “I fear not death—why fear His Majesty!”

entries.zh: 帝遣洛陽令司馬肇策拜芳為貴嬪。
entries.en: Emperor Wu had Luoyang prefect Sima Zhao invest her with honorable rank.
entries.literal: The emperor ordered Luoyang Magistrate Sima Zhao to invest Fang as honorable lady by tally.

entries.zh: 帝每有顧問，不飾言辭，率爾而答，進退方雅。
entries.en: Whenever he questioned her she answered straight without flourish—yet comported herself with modest grace.
entries.literal: Whenever the emperor questioned her she did not polish phrases—answered plainly yet withdrew with modest grace.

entries.zh: 時帝多內寵，平吳之後復納孫皓宮人數千，自此掖庭殆將萬人。
entries.en: After Wu fell he absorbed thousands of Sun Hao’s girls until the harem neared ten thousand souls.
entries.literal: At that time the emperor greatly favored inner chambers; after conquering Wu he took several thousand of Sun Hao’s palace women—thereafter pepper chambers neared ten thousand.

entries.zh: 而並寵者甚眾，帝莫知所適，常乘羊車，恣其所之，至便宴寢。
entries.en: So many favorites he rode a goat cart wherever chance led and slept there.
entries.literal: Many equally favored—emperor knew not whom to choose—often rode goat-drawn cart wherever it pleased, feasting and bedding where it stopped.

entries.zh: 宮人乃取竹葉插戶，以鹽汁灑地，而引帝車。
entries.en: Women sprinkled salt and hung bamboo leaves to steer his goat cart.
entries.literal: Palace ladies therefore inserted bamboo leaves in doors, sprinkled salt water on ground to lure emperor’s cart.

entries.zh: 然芳最蒙愛幸，殆有專房之寵焉，侍御服飾亞于皇后。
entries.en: Hu Fang won nearest monopoly favor—her wardrobe rivaled the empress.
entries.literal: Yet Fang received deepest favor—almost exclusive chamber privilege—attendants’ robes secondary only to empress.

entries.zh: 帝嘗與之摴蒱，爭矢，遂傷上指。
entries.en: Playing dice for arrows she wounded his finger.
entries.literal: Emperor once played chupu with her; quarreling over arrows they wounded his finger.

entries.zh: 帝怒曰：「此固將種也！」
entries.en: He snapped, “That’s pure warrior blood!”
entries.literal: Emperor angrily said: “This truly is general stock!”

entries.zh: 芳對曰：「北伐公孫，西距諸葛，非將種而何？」
entries.en: She shot back, “You marched north against Gongsun and west against Zhuge—what else is warlord stock?”
entries.literal: Fang replied: “North you attacked Gongsun—west you resisted Zhuge—if not general stock, what?”

entries.zh: 帝甚有慚色。
entries.en: He flushed with shame.
entries.literal: The emperor felt deeply ashamed.

entries.zh: 芳生武安公主。
entries.en: She bore Princess Wu’an.
entries.literal: Fang bore Princess Wu’an.

entries.zh: 諸葛夫人名婉，琅邪陽都人也。
entries.en: Lady Zhuge Wan came from Yangdu in Langya.
entries.literal: Lady Zhuge was named Wan, a native of Yangdu in Langya.

entries.zh: 父沖，字茂長，廷尉卿。
entries.en: Her father Zhuge Chong, courtesy Maochang, served as Commandant of Justice.
entries.literal: Her father Chong, courtesy Maochang, was Commandant of Justice.

entries.zh: 婉以泰始九年春入宮，帝臨軒，使使持節、洛陽令司馬肇拜為夫人。
entries.en: In spring 273 she entered court; Emperor Wu had Sima Zhao invest her as Lady from the southern gallery.
entries.literal: In spring of ninth Taishi year she entered palace; emperor faced southern porch and ordered envoy with tally Luoyang Magistrate Sima Zhao to invest her as lady.

entries.zh: 及帝女萬年公主薨，帝痛悼不已，詔芬為誄，其文甚麗。
entries.en: When Princess Wannian died Wu mourned without cease and bid Zuo Fen write—her elegy was splendid.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu’s daughter Princess Wannian died, the emperor grieved endlessly and ordered Fen to compose a dirge—its prose extremely beautiful.

entries.zh: 帝重芬詞藻，每有方物異寶，必詔為賦頌，以是屢獲恩賜焉。
entries.en: He prized her lines; each tribute beast or gem won an ode—she gathered repeated gifts.
entries.literal: The emperor prized Fen’s phrasing; whenever rare treasures arrived he ordered rhapsodies and hymns—thereby she repeatedly received imperial gifts.

entries.zh: 答兄思詩、書及雜賦頌數十篇，並行于世。
entries.en: Her replies to Zuo Si and dozens of essays circulated widely.
entries.literal: Replies to brother Si’s poems, letters, and assorted rhapsodies and hymns—several tens of pieces—all circulated in the age.

entries.zh: 咸寧二年，納悼后，芬于座受詔作頌，其辭曰：
entries.en: In 276 they welcomed Empress Yang Zhi; Zuo Fen took orders at banquet to hymn her:
entries.literal: In second Xianning they brought in Empress Dao; Fen at seat received edict to compose praise, saying:

entries.zh: 惠賈皇后
entries.en: Empress Jia of Emperor Hui
entries.literal: Empress Jia of Emperor Hui

entries.zh: 惠賈皇后諱南風，平陽人也，小名時。
entries.en: Empress Jia Nanfeng of Pingyang—pet name Shi.
entries.literal: Empress Jia of Hui, taboo Nanfeng, native of Pingyang, childhood name Shi.

entries.zh: 父充，別有傳。
entries.en: Her father Jia Chong has his own biography.
entries.literal: Her father Chong has separate biography.

entries.zh: 初，武帝欲為太子取衛瓘女，元后納賈郭親黨之說，欲婚賈氏。
entries.en: Wu favored Wei Guan’s daughter; Empress Yang Yan pushed Jia kin.
entries.literal: At first Emperor Wu wished crown prince to marry Wei Guan’s daughter; Empress Yuan listened to Jia and Guo faction urging marriage with Jia clan.

entries.zh: 帝曰：「衛公女有五可，賈公女有五不可。
entries.en: Wu said, “Wei’s girl scores five merits—Jia’s five flaws.
entries.literal: Emperor said: “Lord Wei’s daughter has five goods—Lord Jia’s daughter five bads.

entries.zh: 衛家種賢而多子，美而長白；
entries.en: Weis are fertile and wise—fair and statuesque;
entries.literal: Wei house breeds wise and many sons—beautiful, tall, fair;

entries.zh: 賈家種妒而少子，醜而短黑。」
entries.en: Jias are jealous and barren—dark and squat."
entries.literal: Jia house breeds jealousy and few sons—ugly, short, dark.”

entries.zh: 元后固請，荀顗、荀勖並稱充女之賢，乃定婚。
entries.en: Yang Yan insisted; Xun Yi and Xun Xu praised Jia’s girl—the match closed.
entries.literal: Empress Yuan pressed firmly—Xun Yi and Xun Xu together praised Chong’s daughter’s virtue—betrothal fixed.

entries.zh: 始欲聘后妹午，午年十二，小太子一歲，短小未勝衣。
entries.en: They first chose sister Wu—twelve, petite beside the heir.
entries.literal: At first they wished to engage younger sister Wu—Wu twelve years old, one year younger than crown prince, too short for robes.

entries.zh: 更娶南風，時年十五，大太子二歲。
entries.en: They wed Nanfeng instead—fifteen, two years his senior.
entries.literal: They switched to Nanfeng—then fifteen, two years elder than crown prince.

entries.zh: 泰始八年二月辛卯[7]，冊拜太子妃。
entries.en: On xinmao in early 272 she became crown princess [7].
entries.literal: Eighth Taishi year second month xinmao [7]—invested crown princess.

entries.zh: 妒忌多權詐，太子畏而惑之，嬪御罕有進幸者。
entries.en: Jealous and scheming, she cowed the befuddled prince—other women seldom touched him.
entries.literal: Jealous, crafty in intrigue—crown prince feared yet dazed—concubines rarely gained favor.

entries.zh: 后遂荒淫放恣，與太醫令程據等亂彰內外。
entries.en: She ran riot with physician Cheng Ju.
entries.literal: Consort then wanton and dissolute—with Imperial Physician Cheng Ju and others licentious noise inner and outer.

entries.zh: 洛南有盜尉部小吏，端麗美容止，既給冢役，忽有非常衣服，眾咸疑其竊盜，尉嫌而辯之。
entries.en: A pretty clerk toiling tombs wore silk—suspected theft.
entries.literal: South of Luo petty clerk of thief corps—handsome bearing—assigned tomb labor yet wore extraordinary clothes—all suspected theft—captain interrogated.

entries.zh: 賈后疏親欲求盜物，往聽對辭。
entries.en: Jia kin listened to his confession.
entries.literal: Consort distant kin sought stolen goods—went to hear interrogation.

entries.zh: 小吏云：「先行逢一老嫗，說家有疾病，師卜云宜得城南少年厭之，欲暫相煩，必有重報。
entries.en: The clerk said, "Going ahead I met an old woman who said her household was ill; diviners said a youth from south of the city should suppress it, and she wished briefly to trouble me, promising rich reward.
entries.literal: Petty clerk said: “Going ahead met old woman saying household illness—diviners said need youth south of wall to suppress—wished borrow briefly—promised rich reward.

entries.zh: 於是隨去，上車下帷，內簏箱中，行可十餘里，過六七門限，開簏箱，忽見樓闕好屋。
entries.en: She rode blindfolded through gates till palaces appeared.
entries.literal: Therefore followed—entered carriage hung curtains—inside bamboo chest—traveled ten-plus li—passed six-seven gates—opened chest—suddenly saw storied towers fine halls.

entries.zh: 問此是何處，云是天上，即以香湯見浴，好衣美食將入。
entries.en: They called it Heaven—bathed and fed him.
entries.literal: Asked where—said Heaven—thereupon fragrant broth bathed—fine clothes fine food led inside.

entries.zh: 見一婦人，年可三十五六，短形青黑色，眉後有疵。
entries.en: A squat dark woman in her mid-thirties bore a brow mole.
entries.literal: Saw one woman—age about thirty-five or six—short form blue-black—scar behind eyebrow.

entries.zh: 見留數夕，共寢歡宴，臨出贈此眾物。」
entries.en: She kept me several nights—we feasted and slept together—and as I left she gave me all these goods."
entries.literal: Detained several nights—slept together feasting—departing gifted many goods.”

entries.zh: 聽者聞其形狀，知是賈后，慚笑而去，尉亦解意。
entries.en: Listeners recognized Jia Nanfeng—the captain dropped charges.
entries.literal: Hearers hearing shape knew it was Empress Jia—left ashamed laughing—captain understood.

entries.zh: 時他人入者多死，惟此小吏，以后愛之，得全而出。
entries.en: Others died visiting her bed—only her pet survived.
entries.literal: Others entering mostly died—only this petty clerk—because consort loved him—escaped whole.

entries.zh: 及河東公主有疾，師巫以為宜施寬令，乃稱詔大赦天下。
entries.en: When her daughter sickened shamans demanded amnesty—she forged pardon.
entries.literal: When Hedong princess fell ill—shamans said broad edicts needed—thereupon forged edict grand amnesty realm.

entries.zh: 初，后詐有身，內稿物為產具，遂取妹夫韓壽子慰祖養之，託諒闇所生，故弗顯。
entries.en: She faked pregnancy—snatched Han Shou’s son Weizu—called him newborn heir.
entries.literal: At first consort feigned pregnancy—packed straw goods as birthing gear—then took sister’s husband Han Shou’s son Weizu raising—claimed mourning-hall birth—therefore not openly shown.

entries.zh: 遂謀廢太子，以所養代立。
entries.en: She meant to replace the heir with him.
entries.literal: Then plotted depose crown prince—establish fosterling.

entries.zh: 時洛中謠曰：「南風烈烈吹黃沙，遙望魯國鬱嵯峨，前至三月滅汝家。」
entries.en: Luoyang sang: "Nanfeng blasts yellow dust—far off Lu towers loom—by the third moon your house will fall."
entries.literal: Then Luoyang rhyme said: "South wind fierce blows yellow sand—far gaze Lu kingdom towering—before third month ends your house."

entries.zh: 后母廣城君以后無子，甚敬重愍懷，每勸厲后，使加慈愛。
entries.en: Lady Guo prized Minhuai—begged Jia to cherish him.
entries.literal: Consort mother Lady Guangcheng because consort lacked sons greatly revered Crown Prince Minhuai—often urged consort—made her add kindness.

entries.zh: 賈謐恃貴驕縱，不能推崇太子，廣城君恒切責之。
entries.en: Jia Mi insulted the heir—Lady Guo scolded him.
entries.literal: Jia Mi relied on pride—could not honor crown prince—Lady Guangcheng constantly scolded.

entries.zh: 及廣城君病篤，占術謂不宜封廣城，乃改封宜城。
entries.en: Ill diviners forbade “Guangcheng”—she became Princess Yicheng.
entries.literal: When Lady Guangcheng gravely ill—divination said unsuitable enfeoff Guangcheng—thereupon changed enfeoff Yicheng.

entries.zh: 后出侍疾十餘日，太子常往宜城第，將醫出入，恂恂盡禮。
entries.en: Minhuai nursed her mother—deferential.
entries.literal: Consort attended illness ten-plus days—crown prince often visited Yicheng mansion—brought physicians—obedient exhaustive ritual.

entries.zh: 宜城臨終執后手，令盡意于太子，言甚切至。
entries.en: She clasped Jia’s hand—beg her shield Minhuai.
entries.literal: Yicheng dying grasped consort’s hand—ordered exhaust feeling toward crown prince—speech extremely earnest.

entries.zh: 又曰：「趙粲及午必亂汝事，我死後，勿復聽入，深憶吾言。」
entries.en: She also said, "Zhao Can and Jia Wu will surely disrupt your affairs; after I die, do not admit them again—remember my words well."
entries.literal: Also said: “Zhao Can and Wu surely ruin your affairs—after I die—never hear them again—deeply remember my words.”

entries.zh: 后不能遵之，遂專制天下，威服內外。
entries.en: Jia ignored—ruled alone.
entries.literal: Consort could not obey—thereupon monopolized realm—awe subdued inner and outer.

entries.zh: 更與粲、午專為姦謀，誣害太子，眾惡彰著。
entries.en: She schemed with them against Minhuai.
entries.literal: Further with Can, Wu solely plotted wickedness—slandered harmed crown prince—crowds of evils manifest.

entries.zh: 初，誅楊駿及汝南王亮、太保衛瓘、楚王瑋等，皆臨機專斷，宦人董猛參預其事。
entries.en: Yang Jun, Sima Liang, Wei Guan, Sima Wei died by her whim—with eunuch Dong Meng.
entries.literal: At first executing Yang Jun and Prince Runan Liang, Grand Tutor Wei Guan, Prince Chu Wei—all improvised executions—eunuch Dong Meng participated.

entries.zh: 猛，武帝時為寺人監，侍東宮，得親信于后，預誅楊駿，封武安侯，猛三兄皆為亭侯，天下咸怨。
entries.en: Dong Meng gained titles—his brothers too—the realm cursed them.
entries.literal: Meng—Wu-era Inner Palace Overseer—served Eastern Palace—won consort trust—participated executing Yang Jun—enfeoffed Marquis Wu’an—Meng three elder brothers all village marquis—all realm resented.

entries.zh: 及太子廢黜，趙王倫、孫秀等因眾怨謀欲廢后[8]。
entries.en: Once Minhuai fell Sima Lun and Sun Xiu used hatred to target her [8].
entries.literal: When crown prince deposed—Prince Zhao Lun and Sun Xiu exploiting resentment plotted depose consort [8].

entries.zh: 后數遣宮婢微服於人間視聽，其謀頗泄。
entries.en: She spied on rumors—some leaked.
entries.literal: Consort repeatedly sent palace maids plain clothes among folk spy listen—plot leaked somewhat.

entries.zh: 后甚懼，遂害太子，以絕眾望。
entries.en: Terrified she murdered Minhuai.
entries.literal: Consort greatly afraid—thereupon harmed crown prince—cutting off hopes.

entries.zh: 趙王倫乃率兵入宮，使翊軍校尉齊王冏入殿廢后。
entries.en: Sima Lun stormed in—sent Sima Jiong to drag her out.
entries.literal: Prince Zhao Lun then led troops palace—ordered Colonel Qi Wang Jiong enter hall depose consort.

entries.zh: 后與冏母有隙，故倫使之。
entries.en: Jiong hated her mother—Lun used him.
entries.literal: Consort with Jiong’s mother bore grudge—therefore Lun sent him.

entries.zh: 后驚曰：「卿何為來！」
entries.en: She cried, “Why you!”
entries.literal: Consort alarmed said: “Why have you come!”

entries.zh: 冏曰：「有詔收后。」
entries.en: Jiong said, "There is an edict to seize you."
entries.literal: Jiong said: "There is an edict to seize you."

entries.zh: 后曰：「詔當從我出，何詔也？」
entries.en: She snapped, "Edicts issue from me—what edict is this?"
entries.literal: Consort said: "Edicts issue from me—what edict is this?"

entries.zh: 后至上閤，遙呼帝曰：「陛下有婦，使人廢之，亦行自廢。」
entries.en: Reaching the upper chamber she cried to the emperor, "Your Majesty has a wife, yet you let others depose her—you will be deposed yourself."
entries.literal: Consort reaching upper chamber cried distant emperor: “Your Majesty has wife yet lets others depose her—you yourself will be deposed.”

entries.zh: 又問冏曰：「起事者誰？」
entries.en: She asked Jiong again, "Who raised this affair?"
entries.literal: Again asked Jiong: “Who raised revolt?”

entries.zh: 冏曰：「梁、趙。」
entries.en: “Liang and Zhao.”
entries.literal: Jiong said: “Liang and Zhao.”

entries.zh: 后曰：「繫狗當繫頸，今反繫其尾，何得不然！」
entries.en: “Chain a dog by the throat—you seized the tail—no wonder!”
entries.literal: Consort said: “Leash dog by throat—now leash tail—how can it not be so!”

entries.zh: 至宮西，見謐尸，再舉聲而哭遽止。
entries.en: Seeing Jia Mi’s corpse she wailed twice—then silence.
entries.literal: Reaching palace west saw Mi corpse—raised voice twice weeping suddenly stopped.

entries.zh: 倫乃矯詔遣尚書劉弘等持節齎金屑酒賜后死。
entries.en: Sima Lun sent Liu Hong with golden liquor.
entries.literal: Lun then forged edict dispatch Minister Liu Hong bearing tally deliver gold-filings wine grant consort death.

entries.zh: 后在位十一年。
entries.en: Eleven years queen.
entries.literal: Consort held rank eleven years.

entries.zh: 趙粲、賈午、韓壽、董猛等皆伏誅。
entries.en: Her cabal died with her.
entries.literal: Zhao Can, Jia Wu, Han Shou, Dong Meng executed.

entries.zh: 妃性酷虐，嘗手殺數人。
entries.en: She killed with her own hands.
entries.literal: Consort nature cruel—often personally killed several persons.

entries.zh: 或以戟擲孕妾，子隨刃墮地。
entries.en: She hurled a ji at a pregnant girl—the infant fell with the blow.
entries.literal: Sometimes threw halberd at pregnant concubine—child fell with blade to ground.

entries.zh: 帝聞之，大怒，已修金墉城，將廢之。
entries.en: Wu rebuilt Jinyong cage ready to depose her.
entries.literal: Emperor hearing greatly furious—already repaired Metal-Walled Fortress—about to depose her.

entries.zh: 充華趙粲從容言曰：「賈妃年少，妒是婦人之情耳，長自當差。
entries.en: Zhao Can soothed him: “She’s young—jealousy passes.
entries.literal: Honorable Lady Zhao Can calmly said: “Consort Jia still young—jealousy is woman’s feeling—long maturity will correct.

entries.zh: 願陛下察之。」
entries.en: May Your Majesty weigh this carefully."
entries.literal: May Your Majesty investigate.”

entries.zh: 其後楊珧亦為之言曰：「陛下忘賈公閭耶？」
entries.en: Yang Zhao added, “Remember Jia Chong?”
entries.literal: Later Yang Zhao also spoke for her: “Your Majesty forgot Lord Jia Chong?”

entries.zh: 荀勖深救之，故得不廢。
entries.en: Xun Xu pleaded—she kept rank.
entries.literal: Xun Xu deeply rescued her—thus avoided deposition.

entries.zh: 惠帝即位，立為皇后，生河東、臨海、始平公主、哀獻皇女。
entries.en: Hui made her queen—mother of Hedong, Linhai, Shiping princesses and others.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui ascended—established empress—bore Hedong, Linhai, Shiping princesses and mournful imperial daughter.

entries.zh: 帝常疑太子不慧，且朝臣和嶠等多以為言，故欲試之。
entries.en: Wu doubted the heir’s wit—He Qiao agreed—so he tested him.
entries.literal: Emperor often suspected crown prince dull—and ministers such as He Qiao said same—so wished to test him.

entries.zh: 盡召東宮大小官屬，為設宴會，而密封疑事，使太子決之，停信待反。
entries.en: He feasted Eastern Palace staff, sealed riddling cases for the heir to solve.
entries.literal: He summoned all eastern palace officials large and small, set banquet, sealed doubtful affairs ordering crown prince to decide—stopped courier awaiting reply.

entries.zh: 妃大懼，倩外人作答。
entries.en: Princess Jia panicked and outsourced answers.
entries.literal: Consort greatly frightened—begged outsider compose answers.

entries.zh: 答者多引古義。
entries.en: Ghostwriters packed classics.
entries.literal: Answerers mostly cited classical meanings.

entries.zh: 給使張泓曰：「太子不學。
entries.en: Clerk Zhang Hong warned, “He never studied.
entries.literal: Orderly Zhang Hong said: “Crown prince does not study.

entries.zh: 而答詔引義，必責作草主，更益譴負。
entries.en: Classic prose exposes the ghostwriter.
entries.literal: Yet reply edict cites meanings—surely will blame draft master—increasing blame.

entries.zh: 不如直以意對。」
entries.en: Plain speech fits better."
entries.literal: Better answer straight from plain intent.”

entries.zh: 妃大喜，語泓：「便為我好答，富貴與汝共之。」
entries.en: She thrilled: "Write plainly for me—wealth and honor we will share."
entries.literal: Consort rejoiced, telling Hong: "Answer well for me—wealth and honor shared with you."

entries.zh: 泓素有小才，具草，令太子自寫。
entries.en: Hong drafted; she made the prince copy.
entries.literal: Hong always had small talent—drafted fully—ordered crown prince himself copy.

entries.zh: 帝省之，甚悅。
entries.en: Wu read it—delighted.
entries.literal: Emperor examined—greatly pleased.

entries.zh: 先示太子少傅衛瓘，瓘大踧踖，眾人乃知瓘先有毀言，殿上皆稱萬歲。
entries.en: He flashed it at Wei Guan—Wei squirmed; courtiers jeered Guan’s prior slanders.
entries.literal: First showed Junior Mentor Wei Guan—Guan greatly ashamed—all knew Guan earlier had slanderous words—hall cheered ten thousand years.

entries.zh: 充密遣語妃云：「衛瓘老奴，幾破汝家。」
entries.en: Jia Chong whispered to the consort, "Old slave Wei Guan nearly ruined your house."
entries.literal: Chong secretly sent word to consort: "Old slave Wei Guan nearly ruined your house."

entries.zh: 后暴戾日甚。
entries.en: Her cruelty mounted daily.
entries.literal: Consort violent cruelty daily worsened.

entries.zh: 侍中賈模，后之族兄，右衛郭彰，后之從舅，並以才望居位，與楚王瑋、東安公繇分掌朝政。
entries.en: Jia Mo and Guo Zhang ran court beside Sima Wei and Sima Yao.
entries.literal: Palace Attendant Jia Mo—consort’s lineage elder; Guards-general Guo Zhang—consort’s maternal uncle—both by talent and prestige held posts sharing governance with Prince Chu Wei and Duke Dongan Yao.

entries.zh: 后母廣城君養孫賈謐干預國事，權侔人主。
entries.en: Lady Guo raised Jia Mi—his power rivaled the throne.
entries.literal: Consort mother Lady Guangcheng raised grandson Jia Mi meddling state affairs—authority matched sovereign.

entries.zh: 繇密欲廢后，賈氏憚之。
entries.en: Sima Yao plotted deposition—Jias feared him.
entries.literal: Yao secretly wished depose consort—Jia faction feared him.

entries.zh: 及太宰亮、衛瓘等表繇徙帶方，奪楚王中候，后知瑋怨之，乃使帝作密詔令瑋誅瓘、亮，以報宿憾。
entries.en: When Sima Liang and Wei Guan banished Yao and clipped Wei’s guard—she forged orders for Sima Wei to murder Liang and Wei.
entries.literal: When Grand Mentor Liang and Wei Guan memorialized to exile Yao to Daifang and strip Prince Chu of central army inspector—consort knew Wei bore grudge—had emperor forge secret edict ordering Wei to kill Guan and Liang—settling old hatred.

entries.zh: 模知后凶暴，恐禍及己，乃與裴頠、王衍謀廢之，衍悔而謀寢。
entries.en: Jia Mo saw danger—planned coup with Pei Yi—Wang Yan backed out.
entries.literal: Mo knew consort fierce—feared disaster reaching himself—with Pei Yi and Wang Yan plotted deposition—Yan repented—plot slept.

entries.zh: 惠羊皇后諱獻容，泰山南城人。
entries.en: Empress Yang Xianrong came from Nancheng in Taishan.
entries.literal: Empress Yang of Hui, taboo Xianrong, native of Nancheng in Taishan.

entries.zh: 祖瑾，父玄之，並見外戚傳。
entries.en: Her grandfather Yang Jin and father Yang Xuanzhi appear among outer kin.
entries.literal: Grandfather Jin; father Xuanzhi—both treated in Outer Kin treatise.

entries.zh: 賈后既廢，孫秀議立后。
entries.en: After Jia Nanfeng fell Sun Xiu debated a new queen.
entries.literal: After Empress Jia deposed—Sun Xiu debated establishing empress.

entries.zh: 后外祖孫旂與秀合族，又諸子自結於秀，故以太安元年立為皇后[9]。
entries.en: Sun Qi’s tie to Sun Xiu won her the throne in 302 [9].
entries.literal: Consort maternal grandfather Sun Qi shared clan with Xiu—sons bonded with Xiu—therefore first Taian year established empress [9].

entries.zh: 將入宮，衣中有火。
entries.en: Fire sparked inside her robes on palace entry.
entries.literal: About to enter palace—fire appeared within robes.

entries.zh: 謝夫人
entries.en: Lady Xie
entries.literal: Lady Xie

entries.zh: 謝夫人名玖。
entries.en: Lady Xie Jiu bore that name.
entries.literal: Lady Xie named Jiu.

entries.zh: 家本貧賤，父以屠羊為業。
entries.en: Her father butchered sheep.
entries.literal: House originally poor low—father by slaughtering sheep practiced craft.

entries.zh: 玖清惠貞正而有淑姿，選入後庭為才人。
entries.en: Pure and lovely—she entered as a talented lady.
entries.literal: Jiu pure kind chaste upright possessing virtuous grace—selected rear chambers became talented lady.

entries.zh: 惠帝在東宮，將納妃。
entries.en: While Hui was heir they chose a princess.
entries.literal: When Emperor Hui in Eastern Palace—about to take consort.

entries.zh: 武帝慮太子尚幼，未知帷房之事，乃遣往東宮侍寢，由是得幸有身。
entries.en: Wu sent her to tutor him in bed—she conceived.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu worried crown prince still young—did not know inner chamber affairs—therefor dispatched go Eastern Palace attend bedding—thereby gained favor pregnant.

entries.zh: 賈后妒忌之，玖求還西宮，遂生愍懷太子，年三四歲，惠帝不知也。
entries.en: Jia drove her west—she bore Minhuai—Hui knew nothing for years.
entries.literal: Empress Jia jealous—Jiu begged return western palace—thereby bore Crown Prince Minhuai—age three four years—Emperor Hui did not know.

entries.zh: 入朝，見愍懷與諸皇子共戲，執其手，武帝曰：「是汝兒也。」
entries.en: Entering court and seeing Minhuai playing with the imperial sons, he took his hand and Emperor Wu said, "This is your son."
entries.literal: Entering court seeing Minhuai playing with imperial sons—grasped his hand—Emperor Wu said: “This is your son.”

entries.zh: 及立為太子，拜玖為淑媛。
entries.en: When Minhuai became heir she became Shuyuan.
entries.literal: When established crown prince—invested Jiu as Shuyuan.

entries.zh: 賈后不聽太子與玖相見，處之一室。
entries.en: Jia barred visits—penned mother and son apart.
entries.literal: Empress Jia did not permit crown prince meet Jiu—housed one chamber.

entries.zh: 及愍懷遇酷，玖亦被害焉。
entries.en: When Minhuai died killers took her too.
entries.literal: When Minhuai met cruel fate—Jiu also murdered.

entries.zh: 永康初，詔改葬太子，因贈玖夫人印綬，葬顯平陵。
entries.en: Yongkang reburied Minhuai—honored her at Xianping.
entries.literal: Early Yongkang—edict reburied crown prince—thereupon granted Jiu lady seals—buried Xianping Mausoleum.

entries.zh: 賈充
entries.en: Jia Chong
entries.literal: Jia Chong

entries.en: Guo Zhang)〉
entries.literal: (Guo Zhang)〉

entries.zh: 楊駿
entries.en: Yang Jun
entries.literal: Yang Jun

entries.zh: 〈(弟珧 珧弟濟)〉
entries.en: younger brother Yang Yao; Yao's younger brother Yang Ji)〉
entries.literal: (Younger brother Yao; Yao's younger brother Ji)〉

entries.zh: 充婦廣城君郭槐，性妒忌。
entries.en: Chong's wife, Lady Guo Huai of Guangcheng, was fiercely jealous.
entries.literal: Chong's wife Lady of Guangcheng Guo Huai was by nature jealous.

entries.zh: 初，黎民年三歲，乳母抱之當閣。
entries.en: When their son Limin was three, his nurse held him near the chamber entrance.
entries.literal: Earlier, when Limin was three years old, the wet nurse held him facing the chamber doorway.

entries.zh: 黎民見充入，喜笑，充就而拊之。
entries.en: The boy brightened when Chong entered; Chong stepped over to pat him.
entries.literal: Limin saw Chong enter, laughed with joy; Chong approached and patted him.

entries.zh: 槐望見，謂充私乳母，即鞭殺之。
entries.en: Lady Guo assumed Chong was sleeping with the nurse and had her flogged to death on the spot.
entries.literal: Huai looked and saw, considered that Chong was intimate with the wet nurse, immediately had her whipped to death.

entries.zh: 黎民戀念，發病而死。
entries.en: The grieving child sickened and died.
entries.literal: Limin's longing and attachment mounted; he fell ill and died.

entries.zh: 後又生男，過期，復為乳母所抱，充以手摩其頭。
entries.en: Another son arrived; after his first month another nurse held him while Chong stroked the infant's head.
entries.literal: Later another boy was born; after the full month, again held by a wet nurse, Chong used his hand to stroke his head.

entries.zh: 郭疑乳母，又殺之，兒亦思慕而死。
entries.en: Lady Guo suspected that nurse too and killed her; the baby died of grief like the first.
entries.literal: Guo suspected the wet nurse; again killed her; the child likewise died longing.

entries.zh: 充遂無胤嗣。
entries.en: Thus Chong was left without male heirs.
entries.literal: Chong thereupon had no heir offspring.

entries.zh: 及薨，槐輒以外孫韓謐為黎民子，奉充後。
entries.en: When Chong died, Lady Guo installed her grandson Han Mi as heir in Limin's place.
entries.literal: When he died, Huai then took grandson-by-daughter Han Mi as Limin's son, to serve Chong's posterity.

entries.zh: 郎中令韓咸、中尉曹軫諫槐曰：「禮，大宗無後，以小宗支子後之，無異姓為後之文。
